# Scan your app, then shield it with a WAF {#sec-lab-08 .unnumbered}

*Exercise 8 · Session 8 lab · Estimated time: 90-120 min*

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
This is the practical task for [Chapter 8: DevSecOps, WAF and secure applications](../chapters/08-devsecops-waf.qmd).
Work through it in your lab group; you talk your answers through at the
session after next (the review runs one session behind). **This page
mirrors the worksheet for reading and reference - the official worksheet
is the PDF distributed via Canvas.**
:::

Write your answers in the answer document `SKY2100_Exercise8_Answers.docx`. Your Nextcloud is encrypted (S6) and the host is hardened (S7). Now you treat it as
an *application* to test and protect. You will run a dynamic (DAST) scan, check for outdated
components, then put a web application firewall in front and watch it block a test attack.

::: {.callout-warning title="Caution"}
Scan and attack only your *own* VM. Sending attack payloads at systems
you do not own is illegal. The test payloads below are harmless probes against your own service.
:::

## Dynamic scan (DAST)

- [ ] **Run an OWASP ZAP baseline scan against your HTTPS Nextcloud (Docker one-liner, or the ZAP GUI).**

  Use the VM's address from `ip a`, not `localhost`: inside the container, `localhost` is the
  container itself.

  ```bash
  docker run --rm -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable \
    zap-baseline.py -t https://<vm-ip>
  ```

- [ ] **Skim the report. Name two findings and their risk level (e.g. missing security header, outdated component). You do not need to fix them all today.**

## Check your components

- [ ] **Open Nextcloud's built-in *Security & setup warnings* (Administration settings $\rightarrow$ Overview) and note any warning or outdated component.**
- [ ] **Why is an outdated dependency an application-security risk, even if *your* code is fine?**

## Put a WAF in front (ModSecurity + OWASP CRS)

- [ ] **Add ModSecurity with the OWASP Core Rule Set to your reverse proxy in front of Nextcloud.**

  A quick route is the official ModSecurity-CRS container, or the Nginx/Apache ModSecurity module. Start
  in *detection* mode (`SecRuleEngine DetectionOnly`), confirm the site still works, then switch
  to *prevention* (`SecRuleEngine On`).
- [ ] **Why start in detection mode before turning on prevention? (one line)**

## Attack your own app - and watch it block

- [ ] **Send a harmless test payload that the OWASP CRS should catch, e.g.:**

  ```bash
  curl -k "https://<your-host>/?q=<script>alert(1)</script>"
  curl -k "https://<your-host>/?id=1' OR '1'='1"
  ```

- [ ] **What HTTP status do you get with the WAF in prevention mode, and what was logged?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Aha"}
Think about what your earlier controls did and did not cover. TLS in Session 6 encrypted the
connection, and the hardening in Session 7 locked down the host, yet the payload you just sent was a
perfectly valid HTTPS request to a port you meant to keep open. Encryption and a firewall cannot see
that the content is an attack, because to them it is normal traffic to an allowed service. That is why
the attack moves up to the application layer, and why the WAF works there: it reads the request itself
and blocks known bad patterns before they reach the app. Note also that the WAF matched a known
pattern, so it is a guard, not a cure. A novel logic flaw it has no rule for would pass, which is why
secure code and scanning still matter.
:::

- [ ] **Read "Tutorial: Create an Application Gateway with a Web Application Firewall" and note how the WAF uses the OWASP rule set.**

  [learn.microsoft.com/azure/web-application-firewall/ag/application-gateway-web-application-firewall-portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/web-application-firewall/ag/application-gateway-web-application-firewall-portal)
- [ ] **Azure WAF runs in *detection* or *prevention* mode. Which one actually protects the app, and why would you ever run the other?**

## Azure reflection

- [ ] **In a DevSecOps pipeline, SAST runs in CI and DAST runs in CD. In one or two lines each, say what each test looks at and why both are needed.**
- [ ] **Your WAF blocked an attack at runtime. Name one application-security control from *earlier* in the SSDLC that should also address the same attack (defence in depth).**

## Knowledge check

1. Why does "the attack move up the stack" to the application after S6 and S7?

   **Hint:** Transit (S6) and the host (S7) are locked, so the application is what remains.
2. Name three OWASP Top 10 categories.

   **Hint:** Broken access control, injection, cross-site scripting - any three.
3. What is the common root cause of injection and XSS?

   **Hint:** Untrusted input treated as code or commands.
4. Why is a vulnerable **dependency** your problem, even with perfect code?

   **Hint:** Most of a modern app is third-party and open-source code.
5. List the five stages of the CSA Secure SDLC.

   **Hint:** Design, coding, build/integrate/test, deliver/deploy, operate.
6. What is **threat modelling**, and when in the lifecycle is it done?

   **Hint:** Finding and ranking threats - done early, during design.
7. Explain "shift left" and why it saves money.

   **Hint:** Move security toward the start; a design flaw is far cheaper than a production one.
8. Define **SAST** and **DAST**, and say when each runs in CI/CD.

   **Hint:** One reads source code before deployment; one probes the running app.
9. What is **SCA**, and what is an **SBOM**?

   **Hint:** It audits your external dependencies for known vulnerabilities; the SBOM is their ingredient list.
10. What does a **WAF** do, and which OWASP resource backs its rules?

    **Hint:** It inspects HTTP at layer 7; its rules come from the OWASP Core Rule Set.
11. Detection vs prevention mode: what is the difference?

    **Hint:** One logs matching requests but lets them through; one blocks them.
12. Why is a WAF "a guard, not a cure"? Give one limitation.

    **Hint:** It blocks known patterns - a novel logic flaw walks straight past.
